fact: Forest covers 85.3% of Mizoram, the highest share of any state; across India it is 21.8% (ISFR 2023).
measure: Forest cover as % of the state's geographical area
compare: India 21.76%; next state Arunachal Pradesh 78.67%; ISFR 2021: Mizoram 84.19%, Arunachal 78.78%
source: Forest Survey of India, India State of Forest Report 2023, Vol. 1, Table 2.4 (Forest Survey of India, MoEFCC)
stays_true: Rank holds in ISFR 2021 and 2023 with a gap of about 6 points; decimals move with each biennial report (ISFR 2025 is the next, due about two years after ISFR 2023).
lead: 6.67 points (8.5%) over Arunachal Pradesh; same lead in 2021 (5.41 points)
size_effect: Share of the state's own area, so size does not drive it. Lakshadweep (UT, 91.33% of 29.63 km2) and A&N Islands (UT, 81.62%) are not states and are left out of the rank.
caution: FSI 'forest cover' means tree canopy of 1 hectare or more at 10%+ density whatever the land's legal status; it includes plantations, orchards, rubber and bamboo, so say 'forest cover', not 'natural forest'.

fact: Six north-eastern states, from Mizoram to Tripura, have forest cover on over 70% of their land; India's share is 21.8% (ISFR 2023).
state: Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Manipur, Nagaland, Tripura
measure: Forest cover as % of state area
value: Mizoram 85.34; Arunachal Pradesh 78.67; Meghalaya 75.65; Manipur 74.28; Nagaland 73.72; Tripura 72.33
compare: India 21.76%; lowest of the six, Tripura 72.33%, is 3.3 times India
source: Forest Survey of India, India State of Forest Report 2023, Vol. 1, Table 2.4
stays_true: All six were also above 70% in ISFR 2021; a state near the line (Tripura 72.3%, Nagaland 73.7%) could slip below 70% in a later report, so recheck against ISFR 2025.
lead: No rank claimed; threshold list. Next state below 70% is Goa at 61.2%.
size_effect: Share of own area; the six range from 10,486 to 83,743 km2.
caution: Threshold facts shift with every edition (check ISFR 2025). Same 'forest cover includes plantations' caution as land-01. Do not add Lakshadweep or A&N (UTs) to the count without saying so.

fact: Goa, India's smallest state at 3,702 km2, has forest cover on 61.2% of its area, against 21.8% for India (ISFR 2023).
measure: Forest cover as % of state area
compare: India 21.76%; Kerala 56.78%; Goa is 2.8 times India
source: Forest Survey of India, India State of Forest Report 2023, Vol. 1, Table 2.4
stays_true: Goa's share has been about 61% in both ISFR 2021 (61.24%) and 2023 (61.20%); next edition ISFR 2025.
lead: No rank claimed beyond being above Kerala (56.78%) by 4.4 points.
size_effect: Smallest state by area, picked because a small state has a large share; share is of own area.
caution: Forest cover counts cashew, coconut and other plantations as well as natural forest; do not call it all 'forest'. Goa is the smallest state by area (3,702 km2, ISFR Table 2.4).

fact: Tree cover is 18.6% of Chandigarh's area, the highest of any state or UT; Delhi is next at 11.9% (ISFR 2023).
measure: Tree cover (patches under 1 ha and scattered trees outside forest) as % of area
source: Forest Survey of India, India State of Forest Report 2023, Vol. 1, Table 2.4 (also stated in the text of section 2.10.4)
stays_true: Chandigarh also led in ISFR 2021 (14.67% vs Delhi 11.53%). Tree cover is re-estimated each ISFR from sample plots; next edition ISFR 2025.
size_effect: Share of own area. A UT of 114 km2, so a small base: say 'state or UT'. J&K and Ladakh are left out (no separate area).
caution: Tree cover is sample-plot based (ISFR prints standard errors in Table 2.13); 2023 tree cover includes bamboo and trees of 5-10 cm dbh. Do not add it to forest cover as 'forest'.

fact: West Bengal holds 2,119 km2 of India's 4,992 km2 of mangroves, 42%; Gujarat is next with 1,164 km2 (ISFR 2023).
compare: 42.45% of India's 4991.68 km2, while West Bengal is 2.7% of India's area; Gujarat 1164.06 km2
source: Forest Survey of India, India State of Forest Report 2023, Vol. 1, Table 3.3
stays_true: West Bengal held 2,117.75 km2 in 2021 and 2,119.16 km2 in 2023 (about 42% both times); the Sundarbans make the gap structural. Next edition ISFR 2025.
size_effect: Not a size effect: Gujarat is 2.2 times larger and has a longer coast (2,340.62 km vs 721.02 km after the 2025 revision).
caution: The report says nothing about causes; do not name the Sundarbans as the reason unless cited separately (it is a fact outside this table). Mangrove cover is a raster-based satellite estimate.

fact: Bamboo-bearing forest in Tripura spans 4,466 km2, equal to 42.6% of the state's area; India's figure is 4.7%.
measure: Bamboo bearing area (inside recorded forest area) as % of state area
column: Bamboo bearing area, ISFR 2023 (km2) / Geographical area (km2) (from land_isfr2023_forest_tree_cover)
source: Forest Survey of India, India State of Forest Report 2023, Vol. 1, Chapter 5 'Bamboo Bearing Area' table; area from Table 2.4
stays_true: Tripura also led in ISFR 2021 (40.06% vs Manipur 37.52%); the gap widened in 2023. Plot-based estimate re-made each ISFR; next edition ISFR 2025.
size_effect: Share of own area, so Madhya Pradesh (20,421 km2, largest in absolute terms) does not lead.
caution: ISFR's bamboo area is measured in sample plots inside recorded forest area only and is not printed as a share of state area: the percentage is our division (numerator inside forest, denominator the whole state). Say 'bamboo-bearing forest area'. Estimates from sample plots with no error printed.

fact: Gujarat has the longest coastline of any state, 2,340.62 km, after the 2025 revision; it was 1,214.70 km before.
compare: 21.1% of India's 11098.81 km, from 5.97% of India's area; next state Tamil Nadu 1068.69 km; old Gujarat figure 1214.7 km
source: Survey of India note 'Length of Coastline of India' (NHO with SoI); Ministry of Earth Sciences, Parliament answer 'Coastline of the Country', PIB 4 Dec 2025
as_on: Revised length promulgated 29 April 2025; Parliament answer 4 December 2025
stays_true: The Government will review the length on a 10-year cycle (Terms of Reference item f), so the next review is about 2035.
size_effect: Coast length is not area; Gujarat's coast share (21.1%) is 3.5 times its area share (6.0%). Andaman and Nicobar Islands (UT) is longer (3,083.50 km) and is left out of 'state'.
caution: Do not say Gujarat's coast 'grew'; the Survey of India says the gap to the old figure is due to scale and method (1:250,000 maps against 1:4,500,000, modern GIS, offshore islands added). Use 'recalculated'.

fact: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands' coastline is 3,083.50 km, 28% of India's, though the islands are 0.25% of its area.
compare: 27.78% of India's 11098.81 km; 0.251% of India's area; Gujarat 2340.62 km; old A&N figure 1,962.00 km
source: Survey of India, 'Length of Coastline of India'; Ministry of Earth Sciences Parliament answer, PIB 4 Dec 2025
stays_true: Next review of the coastline length is on a 10-year cycle (about 2035).
lead: 742.88 km (32%) over Gujarat, the longest state; also longer than the old A&N figure 1,962.00 km
size_effect: Island chains have long coasts for their area; this is the point of the fact, not a hidden size effect.
caution: Coast of an island UT built from peripheral coastline of its islands (India has 1,298 offshore islands/islets in the reconciliation). Never compare with a mainland state's length without saying 'islands'.

fact: In the 2025 revision West Bengal's coastline went from 157.5 km to 721.02 km, now longer than Kerala's 600.15 km.
measure: Length of coastline, old and revised
compare: old 157.5 km (4.6 times smaller); Kerala 569.7 km old and 600.15 km revised; Odisha 574.71 km
source: Ministry of Earth Sciences, Parliament answer 'Coastline of the Country', PIB 4 Dec 2025 (old and revised side by side); Survey of India note
as_on: Revised length promulgated 29 April 2025; Parliament answer 4 December 2025
lead: Revised: 120.87 km (20%) over Kerala; old: Kerala was ahead by 412.2 km
size_effect: Not a size effect: a within-state change between two measurements.
caution: The Survey of India gives one general reason for all states (map scale and calculation method, offshore islands added); it does not explain West Bengal's change separately, so do not suggest a cause, and do not say the coast 'grew'.

fact: Goa has 52 km of coastline for every 1,000 km2 of land, more than three times Kerala's 15 km (revised 2025 coastline).
measure: Coastline length per 1,000 km2 of state area
column: Revised coastline, 2025 (km) / Geographical area (km2) (area from land_isfr2023_forest_tree_cover)
source: Survey of India / Ministry of Earth Sciences (coastline); Forest Survey of India ISFR 2023 Table 2.4 (area)
as_on: Coastline promulgated 29 April 2025; areas as in ISFR 2023
stays_true: Both inputs are fixed until the next coastline review (about 2035).
lead: 36.9 km per 1,000 km2 (239%) over Kerala among states
size_effect: This is a rate per area, built to remove size. Union territories Puducherry (87.0) and Daman and Diu, and the island UTs, are higher and left out of 'state'.
caution: Our division of two official numbers; say 'among states'. Includes the revision (old Goa figure 160.50 km gives 43.4 per 1,000 km2, still the highest state).

fact: West Bengal's 2,216.7 km border with Bangladesh is 54% of that whole border and longer than India's entire Nepal border (1,751 km).
compare: 54.1% of the 4096.7 km India-Bangladesh border; India-Nepal border 1,751.0 km; India-Myanmar 1,643.0 km; next state Tripura 856 km
source: Ministry of Home Affairs, Annual Report 2024-25, Chapter 3 paras 3.5 and 3.9 (length source: Survey of India)
stays_true: Boundary lengths are Survey of India figures that change only by a treaty or survey correction; the report gives the same split for each year.
lead: 2.6 times Tripura (856 km), the next state on this border
size_effect: Border length, not area; West Bengal's border share is 54% while its area share is 2.7%.
caution: Only the Bangladesh and Myanmar borders have state-wise lengths in this report; do not say West Bengal has the longest land border of any state (Nepal and Bhutan lengths are not split by state). Use 'longest Bangladesh border'.

fact: Tripura, 10,486 km2, shares 856 km of border with Bangladesh; Assam, 7.5 times larger, shares only 263 km.
compare: Assam 263 km (7.48 times Tripura's area); per 1,000 km2: Tripura 81.6, West Bengal 25.0, Meghalaya 19.8, Mizoram 15.1, Assam 3.4
source: Ministry of Home Affairs, Annual Report 2024-25, Chapter 3 para 3.9 (Survey of India); area from ISFR 2023 Table 2.4
stays_true: Border lengths are fixed Survey of India figures; Tripura's and Assam's areas are fixed.
lead: Tripura's border is 3.25 times Assam's; Tripura's border per area is 3.3 times West Bengal's
size_effect: This is the surprise: a small state with a longer border than a state 7.5 times larger.
caution: Assam's border also runs with Bhutan (length not split by state in the report); the claim is only about the Bangladesh border.

fact: Sikkim, the second-smallest state at 7,096 km2, touches three countries, as do West Bengal and Arunachal Pradesh, each about 12 times bigger.
measure: Neighbouring countries touched by the state's land border (number)
compare: Countries: China, Nepal, Bhutan. West Bengal (88,752 km2) and Arunachal Pradesh (83,743 km2) also 3; no state or UT touches more; every other border state touches 1 or 2
column: Neighbouring countries whose land border the state touches (number)
source: Ministry of Home Affairs, Annual Report 2024-25, Chapter 3 paras 3.9, 3.16, 3.22, 3.25, 3.26, 3.28 (state lists per border); area from ISFR 2023 Table 2.4
stays_true: Fixed by the boundaries named; changes only with a new state or a boundary treaty.
lead: Tied at 3 with West Bengal and Arunachal Pradesh, so no sole-first claim; Sikkim is 12.5 times smaller than West Bengal and 11.8 times smaller than Arunachal.
size_effect: The point of the fact is the small size; the count is of countries, not length.
caution: The count is our own, from the Ministry's lists of states per border; the report prints no such count. Afghanistan (106 km) is not assigned to any state or UT by the report, so J&K and Ladakh are counted only for what the report names. 'Second-smallest state' is by ISFR Table 2.4 areas (Goa 3,702, Sikkim 7,096, Tripura 10,486).

fact: Uttarakhand has about 105 tigers per 10,000 km2, nearly double the next state, Kerala's 55, in the 2022 estimate.
measure: Tigers per 10,000 km2 of state area
compare: Kerala 54.8; Karnataka 29.4; Assam 29.2; Madhya Pradesh 25.5; India 11.2
column: Tiger estimate 2022 / Geographical area (km2) (area from land_isfr2023_forest_tree_cover)
source: NTCA and Wildlife Institute of India, Status of Tigers, Co-predators & Prey in India 2022, Table I.3.2; area from ISFR 2023 Table 2.4
stays_true: Valid as a statement about the 2022 estimate. The sixth cycle (2026) is under way; a new report is likely to supersede it within about a year, so the figure may be restated.
size_effect: A rate per area; Madhya Pradesh has the most tigers (785) but only 25.5 per 10,000 km2. State rows do not add to India (shared tigers) and West Bengal has no state row.
caution: Rank holds only among the 18 state rows printed. West Bengal (Sundarbans landscape 101, northern WB 2) has no state row so it cannot be ranked. Our division of the report's estimate (SE 24) by the state's total area, not by tiger habitat.

fact: Uttarakhand has 560 of India's 3,682 tigers, 15% of them, on 1.6% of India's area (2022 estimate).
compare: 1.63% of India's area (9.3 times); Maharashtra has 444 on 9.4% of area
source: NTCA and Wildlife Institute of India, Status of Tigers, Co-predators & Prey in India 2022, Table I.3.2; area from ISFR 2023 Table 2.4
stays_true: As land-14: tied to the 2022 estimate; next report likely within about a year.
lead: No rank claimed (Uttarakhand is third by count behind Madhya Pradesh 785 and Karnataka 563).
size_effect: Compares the state's share of tigers with its share of area, so the large states are not favoured.
caution: State rows do not add to the national estimate (3,682, SE 243) because tigers shared between states and outside protected areas are counted once at national level; the share is approximate. Overlaps with land-14; use one of them.

fact: Kerala has about 72 wild elephants per 1,000 km2, the highest density of any state; Assam has 53 (2021-25 DNA-based estimate).
measure: Wild elephants per 1,000 km2 of state area
compare: Assam 53.0; Uttarakhand 33.5; Karnataka 31.4; India 6.8; Kerala has 12.4% of India's elephants on 1.18% of its area
column: Elephant population estimate (number) / Geographical area (km2) (area from land_isfr2023_forest_tree_cover)
source: Wildlife Institute of India, Status of Elephants in India: DNA based SAIEE 2021-2025, Table E.1; area from ISFR 2023 Table 2.4
stays_true: The report calls it a new baseline and expects calibrated methods in future; no next national estimate date is printed, but state-level surveys may be reported meanwhile. Confirm there is no newer release.
size_effect: A rate per area, so Karnataka's larger count does not decide it.
caution: PROVENANCE: the report was read from Mongabay India's hosted copy of the Wildlife Institute of India's PDF, not from wii.gov.in or the Ministry (not found there); confirm before use. The report says the DNA-based figures are not comparable with the 2017 census: no 'decline' claims. Estimate has wide intervals (Kerala 2,378 to 3,193).

fact: Karnataka has 6,013 of India's 22,446 wild elephants, 27% of them, from 5.8% of India's area (2021-25 DNA-based estimate).
compare: 26.8% of India's 22446; 5.83% of India's area (4.6 times); Assam 4159
source: Wildlife Institute of India, Status of Elephants in India: DNA based SAIEE 2021-2025, Table E.1; area from ISFR 2023 Table 2.4
stays_true: As land-16: a new baseline; check for a newer release.
lead: 1,854 elephants (45%) over Assam; confidence intervals overlap (Karnataka 4,792-7,235, Assam 3,395-4,924) only slightly
size_effect: Compares share of elephants with share of area (4.6 times), so Karnataka's size does not explain it.
caution: Same PROVENANCE and 'not comparable with 2017' cautions as land-16. Karnataka and Tamil Nadu also ran their own state counts (2023); do not mix.

fact: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands had 97 wildlife sanctuaries in August 2023, 17% of India's 570; the next, Maharashtra, had 49.
compare: 17.0% of India's 570; 0.25% of India's area; Maharashtra 49; Karnataka 35; Tamil Nadu 33
source: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Rajya Sabha written reply, PIB 10 Aug 2023, Annexure-I (National Wildlife Database Centre, Wildlife Institute of India)
stays_true: A count that rises when sanctuaries are notified (a newer Parliament answer would give a higher total); the lead over the next state is large enough that the rank is unlikely to change, but recheck the count.
size_effect: Counts of sanctuaries; many island sanctuaries are small, so say 'count', not 'area'. Per 1,000 km2, A&N has 11.8 against 0.16 for Maharashtra.
caution: A count, not area; the reply prints no area. Data are for August 2023; a newer reply may have changed the figures. UT, not a state.

fact: Madhya Pradesh (308,252 km2) and Maharashtra (307,713 km2) match in size, but Maharashtra had 1.55 times the people in Census 2011.
compare: Area differs by 539 km2 (0.18%); Census 2011 population Maharashtra 112,374,000, Madhya Pradesh 72,627,000 (1.547 times)
source: Forest Survey of India, ISFR 2023 Table 2.4 (area, Survey of India base); Census of India 2011 population as printed in the National Commission on Population projections report, Table 8 (2011 column)
as_on: Area as in ISFR 2023; population counts as on 1 March 2011
stays_true: Areas are fixed; the Census 2027 count will replace the 2011 populations once released (state this as 'in Census 2011').
lead: MP larger by 539.11 km2 (0.18%); Maharashtra's population 55% higher
size_effect: This is two states of the same size far apart on people, the shape the brief asks for.
caution: Population is a count as on 1 March 2011, not a current figure (the projection report's 2011 column is the Census). Madhya Pradesh's area is 308,252.11 km2 in ISFR (after Chhattisgarh split, as printed).
